newsitem.title: FRANCE: Election results to hit Paris bourse hard -traders.
newsitem.headline: Election results to hit Paris bourse hard -traders.

text.p: French stocks are expected to fall hard on Monday, traders said on Sunday after early projections of the first round of a parliamentary election showed the combined left in the lead.
"I'm not very optimistic for the bourse tomorrow -- few people were expecting results like this," said trader Olivier Blitz at IFF Bourse.
"I expect it to open down at least two percent. If there's little volume, it could drop even more," he said.
Other share analysts forecast even sharply falls of up to five percent for the bourse's blue-chip CAC-40 index.

Projections broadcast as soon as voting ended at 1800 GMT on Sunday gave the opposition Socialists, Communists, extreme-left and other-left candidates between 40.6 and 41.6 percent of the vote, with the ruling RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate-right candidates scoring between 36.1 and 37.1 percent.
"It's bad for the right, and it's just the opposite of what the polls were showing," said salesman Laurent Careno at Kleinwort Benson. "We can easily expect a two percent fall tomorrow," he said.
Bourse operators said the first-round results suggest the runoff next Sunday will be much tighter than had been expected.

The SOFRES polling firm forecast the RPR-UDF coalition would win between 255 and 287 seats, short of the 289 required for a majority. It projected the Socialists would win 250-270 seats, the Communists 21-30 seats and the National Front 0-3 seats.
The BVA institute gave the RPR-UDF 255-275, the Socialists 250-270, the Communists 15-20 and the National Front 0-2.
"The results are very disappointing for the right," said Jacques Chahine, head of his firm Jacques Chahine Finance.
"I expect people to take cover tomorrow. I wouldn't be surprised to see the market fall three to four percent, even with Wall Street's (1.2 percent) rise" on Friday, he said.
He maintains his forecast for a slide to 2,400-2,450 in the CAC if the left wins the runoff, leading to "co-habitation" with a conservative president and a parliament led by the left.
Although the U.S. and British markets will be closed for holidays on Monday, traders expect the big foreign brokerage houses to react on Monday to Sunday's vote results.
U.S. and British investors bought on expectations of a conservative win, said GAN analyst Pascal Nigen. "A lot of them will be disappointed," he said.
The CAC-40 index finished up 21.25 points, or 0.78 percent, at 2,762.90 on Friday -- a gain of nearly 20 percent since the beginning of the year.
Nigen sees the market falling five percent after its recent gains to near records.
A BZW trader said he expects a five percent fall next week.

Credit Lyonnais equities strategist Michelle Jardin said, "We could see a downside correction in the area of five percent next week. Even though the decisive results will be after next week's poll, the market will be nervous," she said.

The franc and the French bond market are also expected to fall on the first-round results, but economist Marie Owen-Thomsen at Banque Internationale de Placements said she expected the stockmarket to react more sharply.
"The bourse risks to see more selling than the bond market, which had pulled back on Thursday and Friday. Bond prices are more realistic," she said.

Jean-Pierre Filbien, director of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Paris, said he expected the bourse to consolidate this week to 2,600-2,650 points on the CAC and fall to as low as 2,350 if the combined left wins the runoff.
He expects defensive stocks with global exposure such as LVMH, Air Liquide, Carrefour and Saint-Gobain to outperform the market.
The most vulnerable stocks are likely to be those in sectors undergoing painful restructurings such as the banking and financial industry and the auto industry, he said.
IFF's Blitz said he expected recent gainers, notably oil majors Elf Aquitaine and Total, to get hit by profit-taking.

GAN's Nigen said he expected Elf, Carrefour, LVMH, and L'Oreal to drop as they had been bought up by foreign investors in recent weeks. He expects bank stocks and carmakers Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen to suffer on concern the Socialists would frown on restructurings entailing job losses.

Careno at Kleinwort Benson said stocks involved in privatisations such as Thomson-CSF and rival bidders Alcatel Alsthom and Lagardere may be hit. "If the Left wins, they could block the privatisation of (the state's 58 percent stake) in Thomson-CSF," he said.
In what promises to be a volatile week, traders said the market will be watching for signs that the conservatives may try to improve their chances by dropping Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
"This looked like a protest vote against Juppe," said Filbien, echoing a commonly heard view.

The bourse's top choice for prime minister would be former finance minister Alain Madelin, a free-marketeer, while some investors, notably foreigners, would be wary of Philippe Seguin, the National Assembly president known for anti-Maastricht views.
"Centrist-sounding" remarks by the Socialists this week would also reassure the markets, Chahine said.

Traders said any effort by the Communists to obtain pledges from the Socialists for ministries in exchange for their cooperation will make the market nervous, as will attacks by the National Front on the conservatives, traders say.
Traditionally, voters for the National Front have tended to tilt toward the conservatives in the runoff vote.
-- Christine Tierney and Pierre Tran, Paris Newsroom, +33 1 4221 5452
